prompt: A service adds one new independent Boolean feature flag. What happens to the number of test cases needed to check every combination of flag settings?

options.explanation: That would test the new flag separately, missing its combinations with existing settings.
Every existing combination can now occur with the new flag either off or on.
Correct. Each old assignment splits into an off case and an on case for the new flag.

options.text: It depends only on the order of the flags
options.explanation: Reordering independent flags does not change their possible value combinations.

workedExample: Keep each existing test assignment and run it twice: once with the new flag off and once with it on. Both settings are independent possibilities. The required coverage therefore doubles, which explains why exhaustive testing grows rapidly.

prompt: Two Boolean health checks, p and q, should trigger an alert exactly when they disagree. Which conditions implement that rule? Select all that apply.

options.text: p has the same truth value as not q
options.explanation: Correct. Matching the negation means the original checks differ.

options.text: not p has the same truth value as not q
options.explanation: Negating both checks preserves agreement, so this alerts on agreement.

options.text: At least one check is true, but they are not both true
options.explanation: Correct. This accepts exactly the two disagreement cases.

options.text: If p then q, and if q then p
options.explanation: Together these implications require agreement, the opposite of the intended alert.

workedExample: The alert should fire when exactly one input is true. Comparing one input with the negation of the other does that, as does requiring at least one input while excluding both. Negating both inputs preserves their agreement; requiring each to imply the other also tests agreement.
